summary: A passage from a novel (Book 11, part 40) in which Aunt Miranda scolds Rebecca for her flowers, hair and finery and insults her late father Lorenzo as a vain, shiftless man who squandered her mother's money. Rebecca defends her father through tears and is sent to bed without supper, while Jane quietly rebukes Miranda for bad manners and bad religion. Miranda is unrepentant but the rebuke lands on her conscience as a storm breaks.
one_line: Aunt Miranda scolds Rebecca and disparages her dead father Lorenzo, and Jane rebukes Miranda as a thunderstorm breaks.
key_facts: Aunt Miranda tells Rebecca she has no patience with her flowers, frizzled-out hair, furbelows and airs and graces, comparing her to her Miss-Nancy father.
Rebecca answers that she will mind quickly when spoken to but will not have her father called names.
Rebecca says her father was a perfectly lovely father and that calling him Miss Nancy is MEAN.
Miranda describes Lorenzo as a vain, foolish, shiftless man who spent Rebecca's mother's money.
Miranda says Lorenzo left Rebecca's mother with seven children to provide for.
Rebecca sobs that it is something to leave seven nice children.
Miranda orders Rebecca upstairs to put on her nightgown, go to bed and stay there until the next morning, with no sound until breakfast time.
Jane tells Miranda that she ought not to have said what she did about Lorenzo, noting that Aurelia always says he was a good husband.
Miranda replies that dead husbands are usually good ones, but the truth needs an airing and Rebecca will not amount to a hill o' beans until some of her father is trounced out of her.
Jane says it wasn't good manners and wasn't good religion, which is one of her annual bursts of courage.
A clap of thunder shakes the house at that moment, and Jane's remark falls on Miranda Sawyer's conscience with a deafening roar.
Rebecca takes off her beloved pink gingham dress with trembling fingers after going up the back stairs.
